claims.text: Thermally activated atomic diffusion is the primary factor governing structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys under high-temperature conditions.
Thermally activated diffusion promotes elemental segregation.
Elemental segregation produces phase inhomogeneities and structural degradation.
The initial nanoalloys are disordered, homogeneous, multielement solid solutions.
Controlled atmospheres minimize extrinsic chemical reactions during annealing.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility and accelerates diffusion kinetics.
Increased atomic mobility causes specific alloying elements to migrate and cluster or segregate at grain boundaries and surfaces.
Segregation creates local compositional fluctuations that disrupt the uniform solid-solution state.
Disruption of the uniform solid-solution state reduces structural stability.
Disruption of the uniform solid-solution state reduces chemical stability.
Higher annealing temperatures and longer dwell times will produce more elemental segregation than annealing at 800°C for 1 hour.
Annealing at 1000°C for 8 hours will be especially likely to produce increased segregation.
Increased segregation will be observable as changes in phase composition by XRD.
Increased segregation will be observable as pronounced compositional inhomogeneity by STEM-EDS.
Higher-temperature and longer-duration annealing will cause mechanical-property degradation relative to the 800°C, 1-hour baseline.
Samples annealed at 800°C for 1 hour are expected to retain a more uniform elemental distribution than samples subjected to higher temperatures or longer dwell times.
Samples annealed at 800°C for 1 hour are expected to retain greater structural integrity than samples subjected to higher temperatures or longer dwell times.
Additional mechanisms may govern behavior outside the stated range of 800–1000°C, a 5°C/min ramp, and dwell times up to 8 hours.
Alternative diffusion paths or kinetic barriers may modify the response within the tested temperature and time regime.
